title: Are the Yankees playing today? See weather forecast for game vs Orioles
description: The Yankees' regular season comes to an end Sunday, whether they play a game or not. See the weather forecast.
fullText:
The Yankees' regular season comes to an end Sunday, whether they play a game or not.

This weekend's nor'easter, which has being wreaking havoc to parts of the New York and New Jersey region, also altered many scheduled start times for MLB games over the past few days.

The Yankees are hosting the Baltimore Orioles this weekend, and the two teams already played a doubleheader on Friday, moving Saturday night's game ahead one day.

162/162. Maybe. pic.twitter.com/UcRN7S3zVk

Sunday's game, the final game of the regular season, was originally scheduled for 3 p.m., like all other MLB games on this day. But MLB allowed the Yankees-Orioles game to be moved up to 1 p.m. because the game has no playoff implications for any team.

Whether they play Sunday's game remains to be seen. Here's the weather forecast:

The rain and wind in the Bronx is expected to increase throughout the day and evening, according to weather.com. Temperatures are in the low to mid 60s. Winds are 18 to 21 mph.

title: Why does Robbie Ure have Robbie Ure on his Scotland shirt?
description: Robbie Ure explains why the back of his shirt read 'Robbie Ure' rather than simply 'Ure' against Slovenia.
fullText:
When Sebastien Pocognoli's first Scotland line-up dropped, there was excitement at the inclusion of Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh for the first time.

Then, the official Uefa teamsheets started doing the rounds in the media box at the Stozice Arena - and there was particular intrigue at Welsh's position of left centre-back and Ure's introduction as 'R.Ure'.

Then, the players came out to face Slovenia and there was only one thing dominating the discourse.

Not Pocognoli's cool and casual cut in the dugout with his cap, or even the debate of whether the away strip is coral, salmon or pink.

Why does Robbie Ure have 'Robbie Ure' on the back of his shirt?

Seldom do footballers - particularly from this neck of the woods - have their full name on their shirt, so it captured the attention of many Scots in a first half they'd rather not focus on anyway.

BBC Scotland asked the 22-year-old the big question after his big day as he wore the number 10 shirt for his country...

Scotland begin Pocognoli era with encouraging Slovenia draw

"A lot of people will just call me, they'll always say 'Robbie Ure'," the Sevilla striker explained.

"They wouldn't just say Ure, so that was a reason.

"And then, to be honest, I think U-R-E is just so small, I just don't really like it.

"So, I put my first name in as well. I've got it at club level too, I just prefer it."

It's his form for club - well, his previous club IK Sirius that earned him his summer move to Spain - that got him here, playing alongside Oli McBurnie as Pocognoli opted for a bold line-up as he made his bow in the dugout.

The aggressive, energetic style the Belgian prefers asks a lot of his strikers. In the three who featured - including Kieron Bowie who replaced Ure after 67 minutes - they have the legs required to do the power of work.

"I loved every minute of it," the former Rangers youth said of his debut. "Obviously, disappointed not to win the game. With the second half performance we probably deserved to but making my debut for Scotland, it's an amazing feeling and I'm really proud and hungry for more.

"The gaffer put the team up on the screen in the meeting and I saw my name. It was a great feeling but I still have a job to do so I tried to keep my emotions quite relaxed."

He might have been hard-pressed to contain his emotions had his long, low drive -the only glimmer of hope in a grim first 45 minutes on Saturday - found the bottom corner rather than caressing the post.

After the break, his pal McBurnie, who "played really well" in his view, had a couple of cracking chances to open his international account on his 17th appearance as the Scots completely dominated.

"We changed the structure up front, I think Oli dropped in a little bit more on the left so was able to play really well with Robbo [Andy Robertson] and Billy [Gilmour], which helped us," Ure explained of the switch at half-time.

"Hopefully our relationship will continue to grow, I really enjoyed it and thought he played really well."

In the end, there were plenty of positives for Pocognoli as his side picked up a point in their Nations League opener.

Plenty for the Tartan Army to take away with them too as a new era begins, with Robbie Ure right part of it.

title: Play-off exit 'hurts' but Peet proud of Wigan side
description: Matt Peet says Wakefield were "far too good" for his Wigan side in Saturday's Super League play-off semi-final, with defeat ending their treble hopes.
fullText:
Matt Peet conceded that Wakefield Trinity were "far too good" for his Wigan side in Saturday's Super League play-off semi-final - but he remains "proud" of the Warriors' team and their achievements this season.

Wigan were aiming to win a second domestic treble in three years, having already lifted the Challenge Cup and League Leaders' Shield, and went into the semi-final on a run of 16 successive victories.

But Wakefield's sensational 33-6 win ended their hopes of a third trophy in 2026 and sent Trinity through to their first-ever Grand Final.

"I'm always proud of the group," Wigan head coach Peet told BBC Radio Manchester after the loss.

"We'll be disappointed with the way it's finished and the time to reflect will be in a few weeks, but I'm proud of the group.

'Pipe dream' to reality? Wakefield reach Grand Final

Wakefield shock Wigan to reach first Grand Final

Hosts Wigan took the lead in the first half with Brad O'Neill's converted try, but Wakefield responded with 33 unanswered points either side of the interval.

"The night 100% belongs to Wakefield," added Peet. "Any time the season finishes, it's sad, but in that manner... we were off but Wakefield played excellent, which made us look that way.

"We were well beaten in every facet of the game and credit goes to Wakefield. We were prepared for a tough game but they were far too good for us."

Wakefield will play Warrington Wolves in the Grand Final at Old Trafford on Saturday, 3 October (18:00 BST).

title: Why latest defeat feels different for Wales
description: Wales may have suffered another Test defeat, but Sean Lynn's new-look side has given fans plenty to be optimistic about before next month's trip to Japan.
fullText:
It was another defeat for Wales, but this one feels different.

As many of the three thousand-plus fans exited Cardiff Arms Park after the USA claimed a 26-24 victory, I assume they did so with a sense of optimism rather than the doom and gloom that often surrounds Welsh rugby.

What head coach Sean Lynn and his backroom staff have done to this group in just six weeks of pre-season is to be applauded.

Wales have been transformed from a side which whimpered out of a winless World Cup and Six Nations into a competitive 80-minute team and one the nation can truly get behind.

Speaking earlier this month, the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) women's rugby director, Nadine Griffiths, said the WXV series would be the real "litmus test" and a "brilliant opportunity to test our progress".

She would have been delighted with the way they obliterated a powerful South Africa side before going toe-to-toe against a USA team ranked inside the world's top six.

Teary-eyed players were naturally disappointed to lose by two points, but it is a sign of the higher standards this group now holds themselves to, and a sign of things to come before they head out to Japan for two further Tests in October.

USA edge past Wales in WXV with Tafuna hat-trick

As it happened: USA earn slender WXV series win over Wales

Wales hooker Kelsey Jones said the players were "disappointed and frustrated" with Saturday's result.

"We left loads out there. Credit to the USA, they were class, but I also think a lot of their success came from our mistakes," she said.

"The girls put in such a shift every week and they are absolutely class. We want to go out, we want to play rugby, that's the most exciting part. We're playing a brand of rugby that we haven't seen from a Wales team in a while.

"It's now about the little fixes, and we've got a big few weeks leading into Japan. Hopefully you've seen that change in the performances."

Wales co-captain Kate Williams said the "overall feeling was just gutted".

"The Test match was there for the taking," she added. "But when we're making that many errors in the championship minutes at the end of the game, we're never going to come out on top.

"We're in these Test matches and we believe that we can win these Test matches. It's going to come right from us. We're going to learn and the next time this happens, it's not going to end like this."

Lynn said "you can see the squad that is building", pointing to his inspirational co-captains Alex Callender and Williams, the discovery of Amy Williams on the wing and Keira Bevan's ability to play at 10.

Young forwards Branwen Metcalfe and Bryonie King have also displayed their Test pedigree, while mainstays such as Georgia Evans, Lisa Neumann and Sisilia Tuipulotu are playing with renewed confidence.

"It's a stable coaching team that we've got now, Gareth Harris coming in as S&C [strength and conditioning]; we've just got to believe in the process," said Lynn.

"I definitely know that we're a lot more competitive and we're being more clinical when we are in those 22 areas."

The reaction of former Wales internationals has also been positive in defeat.

Speaking on BBC One, Philippa Tuttiett said: "Wales were on a run of nine international defeats.

"The turnaround that they have done to beat South Africa and push the sixth-ranked team in the world to the end is incredible.

"It was a tough innings, but still a really proud performance."

Dyddgu Morgan-Hywel said: "We did see the momentum from the South Africa win.

"I was a little worried, but Wales put another performance in. Yes, they're disappointed, but there was only two points in it."

Former captain Siwan Lillicrap said: "I was stood up in commentary and I felt gutted and proud all at the same time.

"I was gutted because they stayed in the fight and could have won it, and proud of the fight they had.

"There were errors; Test match rugby isn't always going to be perfect, but you've got to remember USA are sixth in the world.

"They had an outstanding performance last week, but you learn when you win and you learn when you lose.

"We're still seeing really good stuff and growth from what we've seen previously."

Wales will have a well-earned week off now before returning to camp to prepare for their mini tour of Japan.

They will play two Tests against the Sakura Fifteen; the first in Tokyo on 24 October and the second in Kumagaya City on 31 October.

Wales have won both of their two previous meetings against Japan, who are ranked one place below them in 12th.

But with the humidity and travel to contend with, Wales will have to keep showing signs of progress if they are to continue their upward trajectory - and not only meet the standards they now demand of themselves, but also what we too have come to expect.

title: Scotland & Northern Ireland secure World Cup spots
description: Scotland and Northern Ireland secured qualification for the Netball World Cup after a three-day event in East Kilbride.
fullText:
Scotland and Northern Ireland secured qualification for the Netball World Cup after a three-day event in East Kilbride.

The top two sides from the four-team tournament won their spots in the finals, which take place in Sydney, Australia, with Wales and Republic of Ireland failing to qualify.

Northern Ireland's emphatic 73-50 win in the early match on Sunday meant they would qualify should Scotland win or draw, while Wales' only path to qualification was through a victory over Scotland.

Heading into the final match of the tournament between the Scots and Welsh, the event hosts had their spot in the finals secured unless Wales won with an overwhelming points haul and Scotland ran out 55-48 victors.

The World Cup runs from 25 August-5 September 2027.

title: Czechs beat Ukraine for 12th Billie Jean King Cup title
description: The Czech Republic ease past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time thanks to wins for 2026 Wimbledon finalists Karolina Muchova and Linda Noskova.
fullText:
Czech Republic eased past Ukraine to win the Billie Jean King Cup for the 12th time.

This year's Wimbledon finalists Linda Noskova and Karolina Muchova breezed past their opponents to secure a 2-0 victory and deny the Ukrainians a first title in the competition.

Muchova, the runner-up at Wimbledon, comfortably beat Anhelina Kalinina 6-2 6-3 in the opening singles match before Noskova's 6-3 ⁠7-6 (7-5) win over world number seven Elina Svitolina ‌secured the title.

It is the Czechs' first win at the event since 2018, making them the second-most successful nation in its history after the United States, who have 18 titles.

It was also a first win as captain for Barbora Strycova, who has three previous triumphs to her name as a player. As a team, they dropped just one set throughout the tournament.

The Czechs also knocked out Great Britain in the quarter-finals in Shenzhen, China, which led GB captain Anne Keothavong to describe them as "the strongest team here".

title: Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
description: Ethiopian runner Tigst Assefa wins the Berlin Marathon but narrowly misses out on breaking the women's world record because of injury.
fullText:
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.

The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.

But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.

Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.

Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.

However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.

In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.

"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.

"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.

"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."

The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.

Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

title: USA's new breakout star? Sullivan living up to Premier League promise
description: Cavan Sullivan made his United States debut on Saturday aged just 16 - and produced a performance to show just why Manchester City moved to sign him.
fullText:
With a little over a year to go before he can officially join Manchester City, United States wonderkid Cavan Sullivan has taken his next step towards the big time.

At 16 years and 363 days, the Philadelphia Union midfielder became the fourth youngest player to play for the USA - starting Saturday's 4-1 friendly win over Peru.

Ever since City moved to secure the future signing of a then 14-year-old Sullivan back in 2024, there has been plenty of intrigue around his progress, and hype to go with it.

It led to a level of expectation rarely seen around a young American player - reinforcing the sense that he might be the real deal.

Manchester City saw something in him and were willing to wait for that potential to be realised at senior level. His MLS team, Philadelphia Union, have also shown patience as they gradually introduced him to senior football.

His first run of regular starts for Union came as the 2026 MLS season resumed post-World Cup, and that first international call-up soon followed.

There is one complication, though - the ongoing news around his future club. He made his international debut the day after City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching. The club are expected to appeal.

His performances, goals, and assists since the World Cup put him up there with the MLS's top individual stars, including Lionel Messi, Antoine Griezmann and Luis Suarez.

Few players beyond those mentioned can match Sullivan's goal contribution rate in MLS since the World Cup, and there is a strong argument to say the youngster has been the best player in the league during that time.

The numbers speak for themselves.

They speak of a player who has performed a key role in his team's rise up the league table in the past few months, and of one who has the output in front of goal to go with the minutes on the pitch.

The facts need no extra hype or sensational Messi comparisons. Sullivan has seven goals and five assists in MLS this season. Six of those goals and four of those assists have come during August and September.

Sullivan has scored six goals in the past six games, and has been named in the league's Team of the Matchday a total of seven times, including for the past three consecutive matchdays.

Is he the breakout soccer star that the United States have long been desperate for? He is about to become a big part of that conversation.

As the expectation rises, there has to be caution when discussing a player who only turns 17 this month.

"It's well known that Americans are drawn to stars in sports, and as the World Cup showed, that applies to soccer too," Jonathan Tannenwald, chief soccer correspondent for the Philadelphia Inquirer, told the BBC.

"So it's no surprise that the country hopes for a star in men's soccer to match the many it has had in women's soccer.

"I'm not going to say today that Cavan Sullivan is going to be that player. It's too early to know for certain, and I've seen plenty of names not make the grade.

"Freddy Adu is among the infamous, but there are others, such as Gedion Zelalem at Arsenal. Christian Pulisic has come closest, but isn't really there and had a worse World Cup than hoped for. Gio Reyna has never measured up to his talent.

"What I will say about Sullivan is he has the work ethic to go with the talent. As his current manager at the Philadelphia Union, Ryan Richter, said recently, external: 'His outstanding quality is the mentality that he has, and the way that he approaches every game and every day, and that's what pushes him to get better and better.'"

Sullivan's full-time introduction to the Philadelphia Union team has coincided with a turnaround in their season, led by interim coach Richter, who took over before this post-World Cup run-in.

They are unbeaten in 11 games, winning nine. This is in stark contrast to the beginning of the season when they only won one game in 15. Sullivan has played a key part in this improvement.

During this time, Sullivan has been playing in a right-sided attacking midfield role, but with the freedom to drift as a central number 10 might and cut inside on his stronger left foot.

He has a good all-round game, and also has good strength relative to his age. He is not quite at the level an emerging Wayne Rooney was as a teenager at Everton, but his physicality that means he can more than hold his own in a robust league such as MLS.

Rather than struggle with the weight of expectation, his performances have improved as the spotlight on him has brightened.

It appears he is already outgrowing the North American league, but it might be wise to allow him to play at this level, in his hometown, with his family around him (his brother Quinn, 22, also plays for the Union) for a little while longer, regardless of the other options open to him pre-City.

"I find him to be handling the pressure of everything pretty well," added Tannenwald.

"Talk with him for long enough, and you'll know he's still a teenager, still finding his way with some things as any teen would.

"Yes, he can come across as cocky, but he's well grounded, not just by Richter, but by having his oldest brother there in the locker room with him.

"Away from the stadium, Sullivan has a strong family at home. Both of his parents, Brendan and Heike, played soccer, and grandfather Larry went from a player in the 1960s to one of the most famous coaches in the Philadelphia region.

"They all keep Cavan grounded too, even as they know he is the best of all of them."

title: Parsons becomes record try scorer as Ireland beat Japan
description: Beibhinn Parsons becomes Ireland women's all-time record try scorer as they hold off a late comeback from Japan to register a 31-24 win in the WXV Global Series at Dexcom Stadium.
fullText:
Tries: Hogan (2), Parsons (2), Dalton Cons: O'Brien (3)

Tries: Nagaoka (2), Nagata, Asari Cons: Nishi (2)

Beibhinn Parsons became Ireland women's all-time record try scorer as they held off a late comeback from Japan to register a 31-24 win in the WXV Global Series at Dexcom Stadium.

Tries from Brittany Hogan and Parsons gave the home side the lead after a dominant first half.

Japan looked strong after the restart before Parsons registered her 24th Test try to take the scoring record and help them secure the win.

Scott Bemand will be happy with his side's response after they let a 19-point lead slip away against the USA in their WXV Global Series opener at Tallaght Stadium.

Both sides had to navigate a strong wind in Galway, and it was Ireland who adjusted to the challenging conditions the quickest with Hogan showing great persistence to cross from close range after 10 minutes.

It was a scrappy first half with plenty of stoppages and neither side able to carve open the opposition's defence.

Hogan once again showed her threat and extended Scott Bemand's side's lead when she finished a nice move from Aoibheann Reilly after the half-hour mark.

A mistake in the Ireland defence then gifted Japan a great opportunity to register their first try before Anna McGann rushed back to stop Nami Asari's run.

The home side extended their lead after a superb solo run from Parsons in her home town on 37 minutes.

Following captain Erin King's yellow card, Japan scored a late first-half try when Moe Nagaoka crashed over.

Japan started the second half brightly and Nagaoka crossed from a maul to narrow Ireland's lead.

Unlike against the USA, Bemand's side responded well to the setback and Aoife Dalton touched down just minutes after coming off the bench.

The end-to-end nature of the match continued with Japan continuing to push and Nijiho Nagata able to register Japan's third try from a maul.

Parsons then produced another impressive run after connecting with McGann's pass, with O'Brien able to add the extras.

In the closing stages, Asari narrowed Ireland's lead after the home side had originally done well to stop the visitors from crossing, but Japan could not produce an impressive late comeback.

Ireland: Flood; Parsons, McGann, Higgins, Elmes Kinlan; O'Brien, Reilly; O'Dowd, Jones, Cahill; Wall, Tuite-O'Sullivan; Hogan, King (capt), Adams Verling.

Replacements: Buttimer, McGrath, Djougang, Clohessy, Moore, Lane, Dalton, Gallagher.

Japan: Nishi; S Nishimura, Kataoka, Furuta, Imakugi; Harada, Tsukui (capt); Komaki, Nagaoka, Kitano; Kawamura, Sato; Asari, Korai, Nduka.

Replacements: Nagata, Yoshida, Fuji, Yoshimura, M Nishimura, Seo, Yamamoto, Havili Kagawa.

title: Horner a distraction for Ferrari says Vasseur
description: Christian Horner is proving a distraction for Ferrari by "looking for a job", team principal Frederic Vasseur says.
fullText:
Christian Horner is proving a distraction for Ferrari by "looking for a job", team principal Frederic Vasseur says.

Horner, dismissed as Red Bull team principal in July 2025, used an interview with the Times this week to say that Ferrari are the only Formula 1 team he would work for without being given a shareholding, describing it as "the dream", external.

Vasseur outlined his frustration with Horner following Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix - at which Charles Leclerc finished fourth and his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton was sixth.

He said: "We are not working in the perfect serenity.

"For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, it's a bit of a frustrating situation.

"We are fighting for P3 [third place] in the championship, and at the end of the day, we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have.

"But it is what it is, it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated, focus on what is better today."

After the race in Baku, Hamilton was asked by Sky Sports whether he was confident Ferrari were on a good path under Vasseur's leadership. The seven-time champion replied: "Yes."

Vasseur was asked whether he was joking about Horner, and replied: "I was very serious."

And asked whether he would consider working with Horner, he replied: "This you have to ask my assistant."

That remark appears to be a reference to the circumstances surrounding Horner's departure from Red Bull in July 2025.

Horner was accused of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour by a female employee. The allegation became public in February 2024 but the accusations were dismissed by Red Bull following two internal investigations.

Horner was fired from his role as chief executive officer and team principal by Red Bull after the 2025 British Grand Prix.

That decision followed a tumultuous 18 months in the wake of the employee's allegations, during which a number of senior team figures left - including chief technical officer Adrian Newey - and there was a slump in form.

Red Bull have never given a public explanation for Horner's dismissal. The two parties agreed on a settlement said by sources to be worth 60m euros (£51.5m).

Ferrari entered this season hoping to be title contenders following the introduction of new chassis and engine rules in F1.

But while their car was acknowledged as the best in the corners as the season began, their engine has lacked performance compared to those of Mercedes and Red Bull.

This lack of power was exposed on the long straights of the Baku circuit, as Leclerc slipped back in the race after qualifying second.

Vasseur said on Saturday: "With the situation that we are in the engine, we are losing one position per lap, and then we lose the path of the race.

"Honestly we were surprised to be in the first row, because Baku is the most demanding in terms of engine, and was not expecting to do so. But we knew even starting from the first row that the opening laps, or in case of restarting safety car and so, it would be difficult. And it was."

Asked whether he was still committed to his position at Ferrari, Vasseur said: "Motorsport is my life, it's my business. I'm trying to do my best. I'm there to do my job. I have the best job in the world, heh. But, it is like it is. We have still seven races to go, and I will push until the last corner."

Ferrari have not won a world championship since 2008, and have rarely had a fully competitive car since then.

Horner said in his interview: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

title: Why Premier League faces uncertainty and chaos after Man City ruling
description: It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been made on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City. Here's what it means.
fullText:
If you were getting the impression that the saga over Manchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again.

Two years and 10 days since the hearing began, and 1,329 days after City were charged, we now know a verdict has been reached, with the club guilty of the majority of financial rule breaches.

That is not because the Premier League or Manchester City have told us - it is thanks to the Athletic finding out and breaking the story., external

BBC Sport was later told the verdict was sent during the week to club executives, who had to sign a non-disclosure agreement to open the file.

A process can appear to be completely watertight, as this one certainly had been, but when the circle of trust is expanded, the chance of information getting out increases.

Despite this, public silence from the Premier League continues.

City did not address whether they had been found guilty in a statement making it clear - with an appeal expected - that the "process remains ongoing" from their point of view.

It all points to the suggestion that the long-awaited decision of the independent panel was not a case of this process nearing an end, but perhaps instead reaching the end of the beginning.

It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now.

City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion.

The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who have always insisted they have done nothing wrong.

When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole.

And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation.

Enzo Maresca's side go to Liverpool on 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless?

Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing.

No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains

Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case.

As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel.

BBC Sport has been told this hearing could still be months away, and the result may not be published until the appeal is completed.

At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion.

This differs from Chelsea's case earlier this year, as the Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement.

It is possible that City could decide to hold their hands up and try to agree a deal - which would be better for the league - though that seems unlikely given the club's consistently strong denials over many years.

The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment.

Remember, Everton were docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Nottingham Forest were deducted four points.

These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions.

This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty.

That is before you get into the inflated sponsorship revenue allegedly channelled through the companies' accounts as a means of meeting financial fair play rules, payments to players and managers, and a failure to comply with investigations.

Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018.

Chelsea and Manchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. While Chelsea admitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted.

And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition?

Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely.

So what if Manchester City win the league?

Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season?

This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition.

There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this.

But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment.

Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation

Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict

Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow

The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal.

It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation.

Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season.

It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs.

The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard.

Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases.

But, as ever in this case, the complexities indicate this is not straightforward.

There is the chance, though slim, that the punishment is only applied to the league table after the appeal.

That would surely lead to protests from impacted teams this season, who will demand it should, as usual, come into effect immediately.

Manchester City vs The Premier League

For the integrity of the Premier League, so all clubs know what they are playing for, this would need to happen sooner rather than later.

Last season, a points deduction for West Bromwich Albion related to breaches of profit and sustainability regulations was not announced until 24 April.

While ultimately they stayed in the Championship, it plunged them back into a relegation fight when they thought they were safe. It also gave some hope to the teams in the relegation zone.

The Premier League does not want this to drag on until the penultimate month of the season, but nothing is guaranteed in this story.

In this scenario, let's not forget City could also win their appeal, like they did over Uefa's punishment back in July 2020.

While this would be celebrated at Etihad Stadium it would likely not be the end of the acrimony over the case.

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation from Manchester City over the case.

One source, who held a senior executive position at two Premier League sides, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.

Another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league.

Premier League rules allow clubs to seek legal action against each other for compensation.

In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley £35m after they broke PSR over a three-year period.

Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.

Everton are appealing, with sources previously saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.

There is uncertainty over a statute of limitations, which would set a cut-off point for claims.

Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham Hotspur reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation two years ago.

This is not just about Manchester United (twice) and Liverpool, who finished as runners-up to City in their title-winning seasons.

It is about those clubs who just missed out on the Champions League, or failed to make Europe, or even those who were relegated.

And it could even result in claims over the prize money for each Premier League place, or the potential commercial earnings lost by rival clubs.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport it would be considered a "denial of an opportunity" by complainants.

Maguire explained that the "statute of limitations is not referenced" in the Premier League's traditional handbook, though that could be subject to a legal challenge from City.

But what of the compensation? Just looking at Champions League qualifying could bring huge financial claims.

"The Champions League in those days was worth a minimum of £30m," Maguire said. "I think by the time we got to 2018, it was probably worth £60m or £70m, and that's in prize money.

"On top of that, you could claim for loss of gate receipts, loss of sponsor bonuses. This is highly unlikely, but it's certainly being discussed.

"Players get bonuses for qualifying for the Champions League. Those bonuses, if you talk to people connected to the elite clubs, are normally in the region of 25%.

"An average salary in those days would probably, if you go back to 2012, be in the region of £80,000 or £90,000 a week. Twenty-five percent of that is four or five million pounds a year. That's how the issues stack up."

Points deductions, fines, and compensation claims.

This is an extremely messy situation for the Premier League, and it does not look like being resolved anytime soon.

title: Berlin Marathon 2026 results and times after Tigst Assefa and Guye Adola triumph in major
description: The iconic marathon major saw Ethiopian runners Tigst Assefa and Guye Adola secure wins under the Brandenburg Gate
fullText:
Tigst Assefa wanted her world record back and was on course to smash it until cramps before the finish line dashed her hopes in the Berlin Marathon on Sunday.

The 29-year-old Assefa still ran the third fastest time ever. She set a new course record with an unofficial time of 2 hours, 11 minutes and 4 seconds for her third Berlin Marathon win after 2022 and 2023.

Assefa set a world record with her time of 2:11:53 in 2023, only for Ruth Chepng'etich to lower the mark by nearly 2 minutes to 2:09:56 in Chicago the following year.

Chepng'etich wasn't racing Sunday because she's serving a three-year ban for a doping violation. Her record still stands.

Assefa was well on course to beat Chepng'etich's time, but the Ethiopian runner pulled up with cramps before reaching the Brandenburg Gate and limped over the finish line, where she slumped to the ground and fought back tears.

Second-placed Bedatu Hirpa was almost 6 minutes behind, followed by another Ethiopian, Dera Dida.

The 35-year-old Guye Adola of Ethiopia won the marathon by crossing the line in an unofficial time of 2:02:50. It was his second win in the German capital after his victory in 2021.

Gemechu Dida Diriba of Ethiopia was second, 28 seconds behind, followed by Gabriel Gerald Geay of Tanzania.

World record holder Sabastian Sawe was unable to take part because of an injury, but he was a guest of honor at the event.

Start times were brought forward Sunday because of high temperatures in last year's marathon. Conditions were almost perfect with autumn sunshine and little wind, though it was still warm.

title: White Sox at risk of wasting $20M if trade deadline pickup can't turn things around
description: This White Sox pitcher could be a $20 million waste if 2027 isn't a bounce-back year.
fullText:
White Sox at risk of wasting $20M if trade deadline pickup can't turn things around originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Chicago White Sox went out and acquired some pitching help at the MLB trade deadline this summer, acquiring some reliever help, but most notably, adding Luis Castillo from the Seattle Mariners.

They spent a lot to get him, not only in the capital they sent to the Mariners, but also in what they owe Castillo. They agreed to take on his full remaining contract, which could make his $20M contract a major mistake.

As USA Today's Bob Nightengale highlighted, they might've wasted that $20 million on Castillo if he cannot figure things out next season. A lot of money is on the line with Castillo, and there's reason to worry in Seattle.

"The Chicago White Sox, who grabbed Luis Castillo at the trade deadline, need to find a way to fix him 2027 or else they just wasted $20 million," Nightengale writes.

Adding Castillo wasn't a terrible idea for the White Sox, as there was hope he'd be able to turn back the clock and perform well after a change of scenery.

While the change of scenery did lead to a change in production from the mound, it was in the complete opposite direction of where the White Sox needed it.

In 20 outings with the Mariners, Castillo posted a 5.06 ERA. It was a first-half season stint with a -0.6 bWAR for Castillo, extremely underwhelming for someone who's been an All-Star pitcher with a 3.54 and 3.64 ERA in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

MORE: White Sox reportedly have 'no urgency' to sign Munetaka Murakami to an extension

But things got a lot worse with the White Sox. In nine outings, Castillo managed to accrue -0.9 bWAR thanks to a horrible 8.42 ERA across 31 innings pitched.

Unfortunately, Castillo has been a net negative for the White Sox. To make matters worse, the White Sox are locked into Castillo for the 2027 MLB season for the final year of his five-year, $108 million contract.

This is a poor situation for the White Sox, as their big trade deadline pickup might become a huge waste for Chicago. If he can't figure things out for the 2027 season, Castillo will be a major blemish on an otherwise exciting White Sox team.

title: DOE releases national quantum computing roadmap
description: Quantum computing is becoming a revolutionary tool for scientific discovery.
fullText:
Quantum computing is becoming a revolutionary tool for scientific discovery.

Editor’s note: The following article was originally published by the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science. Fermilab played a key leadership role in developing the SCAC Quantum Committee Report. Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and associate laboratory director for the Technology Directorate, chaired the Quantum Subcommittee and Supratik Guha, professor at the University of Chicago’s Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering, served as vice chair. Together with the subcommittee, they led an extensive stakeholder-engagement process that drew perspectives from national laboratories, academia, industry and federal agencies, informed by input from hundreds of contributors across the U.S. quantum ecosystem.

The report lays out a science-first, milestone-driven roadmap toward demonstrating scientific utility from quantum computing, while building toward the integration of quantum systems with the DOE labs’ research infrastructure, high-performance computing and artificial intelligence.

Fermilab thanks the SCAC Quantum Subcommittee members and the many quantum researchers and stakeholders who contributed their time, ideas and expertise. With this report as a foundation, Fermilab looks forward to working alongside partners across the national quantum ecosystem toward an integrated quantum future and the next era of scientific discovery.

Every major shift in technology promises to redefine the boundaries of discovery. Quantum computing is rapidly transitioning from a phase of fundamental laboratory research into a scientifically revolutionary capability. As this technology races forward, we need a clear, defined path to success. That is why I charged the Office of Science Advisory Committee (SCAC) Quantum Subcommittee with an ambitious task: to chart a milestone-driven roadmap toward demonstrating a scientifically relevant, error-corrected quantum computer by 2028, and to articulate a long-term vision for a dedicated Quantum Computing User Facility.

Today, I am proud to share their newly released report, “SCAC Quantum Committee Report: Path to an Integrated Quantum Future.” It confirms what many of us in the scientific community have felt: we have reached a historic inflection point.

Our mission now is to ensure the United States leads this next era of discovery.

For years, the quantum conversation has been dominated by hardware-centric milestones. While these metrics are vital, the SCAC report proposes a crucial shift in thinking: success must be measured by scientific utility.

Our goal is not simply to build the largest quantum computer; it is to solve problems that are otherwise completely intractable. We are talking about predicting exact molecular properties for drug discovery, designing transformative catalysts for manufacturing, simulating fusion-relevant materials, and modeling the fundamental physics of the early universe.

The report emphasizes that the Department of Energy is uniquely positioned to lead this transition. By leveraging our world-class National Laboratories, high-performance computing (HPC) centers, testbeds, and existing scientific User Facilities, we can integrate quantum processors directly into hybrid, classical-quantum workflows that accelerate real-world discovery.

To achieve scientifically useful quantum computers, the SCAC recommends a highly strategic, three-phased framework that aligns with our national Quantum Genesis Initiative:

To realize this future, we must break down traditional barriers. The SCAC report highlights that breakthrough science occurs when hardware developers and domain scientists work side-by-side. We are actively exploring novel partnership models, which could include embedded co-design fellowships, joint appointments, and shared technical staff across industry and our National Labs.

Crucially, we must maintain a technology-neutral stance. The field is evolving too quickly to prematurely lock in a single hardware modality. Whether through superconducting circuits, neutral atoms, trapped ions, photonics, or spin qubits, we will let demonstrated scientific utility guide our long-term investments.

I want to express my deepest gratitude to the Subcommittee Chair, Dr. Anna Grassellino, Vice-Chair Dr. Supratik Guha, and the hundreds of stakeholders from industry, academia, and federal agencies who contributed to this report.

We stand at a pivotal moment. The choices and investments we make over the next three years will shape global scientific leadership for decades to come. Together, we are not just building quantum computers; we are establishing a new national capability for scientific discovery.

Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory is America’s national laboratory for particle physics and accelerator research. Fermi Forward Discovery Group manages Fermilab for the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science. Visit Fermilab’s website at www.fnal.gov and 

DOE’s Office of Science is the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States and is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time.

title: postmarketOS Rebrand: Nura
description: Aiming for a 10 year life-cycle for smartphones
fullText:
After a one and a half year selection process, the new name of the operating system formerly known postmarketOS has been announced during the mystery talk of our very own conference. From now on this project is known as Nura!

Through the years, most members of the team have experienced difficulties doing outreach for "postmarketOS" due to the complexity of the name. The name is long and can be very hard to pronounce in many languages. This also has the implication that it gets very hard to remember in those same languages.

The capitalization is also grammatically awkward, with lower-case "p" and "m" but upper-case "OS". We have seen Postmarketos (PostMarketOS?, PostmarketOS?, post-market OS?) written in too many ways, which is confusing to both the reader and the writer.

Finally the name is descriptive. Although that can help people understand what the project is about, it also limits the scope of the project in ways that were out-of-touch with reality long ago, for example when PINE64 sold PinePhones with postmarketOS pre-installed. What was initially an asset, became a liability after all these years. The name being descriptive also means it cannot be trademarked. We believe trademarks can be important, as it allows the project to protect users against fraudulent uses of the name, or users clearly misaligned with the project goals. A trademark for the new name has already been filled.

All in all, "postmarketOS" has served us very well, it brought us to where we are now, and will always be part of our history. At the same time, we believe that to make the project better known outside the hacker community, a rename to a name with less meaning and easier to write, pronounce, and remember would be of benefit of the project.

Yes, we really like the logo and its connection with our mission, and we don't see a need for a change, regardless of the rename.

Changing something that is core to the project identity, like its name, is not something done lightly. Our initial process did not produce the consensus that we expected, so we came up with new approach that resulted in this new name. We have also been waiting for trademark lawyers, and eventually it made sense to wait some weeks to announce it at our conference.

Although there is no public site in Nura.org, the domain is taken. We sent an offer to the owner through a broker, but the owner did not consider selling it for a reasonable price. We looked for alternatives and found the eco domain, which we like even more now! Eco is short for ecology and the intended use is: ".eco is open to organizations, businesses and people committed to positive change for the planet". The .eco domain has strong policies which prevent abuse of the domain for greenwashing, adding another layer of accountability. It just fits perfectly with our mission and goals.

A selection team composed by Pablo, Pan, Ranny, and Sriram Ramkrishna (thank you all!) was tasked to select good names that would meet the criteria from the 300+ the community shared with us. The team did multiple rounds through the list, evaluated pros and cons of different names, and came up with a proposal of 4 names for the team to choose from. Those names went through further triaging to make sure it didn't have very problematic connotations in as many languages as we could find speakers, from all continents. All of them passed the criteria, and where put to a vote within the team using range voting. Nura was the name with the highest value, and received a 0.4 mean for a vote between -2 and 2. It was therefore chosen as our next name.

Yes, there are some small updates to the logo! Ranny identified and fixed some small design inconsistencies in the logo, and we used the name change as an opportunity to update it too. Due to slightly more spacing between the arrows, it is now a bit more legible from further distances. Furthermore it is also now mathematically constructed, so anyone can reproduce it!

The renaming of all user-facing strings might take a while. If you notice a place where we missed something, any contribution in the form of Merge Requests to update it to Nura would be super helpful. If you notice it is taking a while to update, and you do not have the skills to update it, opening issues to remind the team would also be welcomed.

title: US Military disables ad trackers amid concerns over troops' safety
description: The new security measures come after commercial data was used to track and target U.S. forces in the Middle East.
fullText:
The U.S. military has disabled advertising tracking tools in government-issued phones, computers and other devices, officials recently told Congress.

The different military branches confirmed they had done so, some only this summer, following reporting that commercially available data taken from these devices and sold freely by data brokers, was being used by Iran and other adversaries to track and in some cases target American bases and personnel. The confirmation came from a letter shared by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC). The letter calls on the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General to review department security guidelines. Wyden and others revealed in a similar letter in May that foreign groups were using commercially available location data to target U.S. troops.

“The sale of location data, particularly that of U.S. government personnel, poses a serious threat to national security,” Wyden wrote.

According to Wyden and Harrigon’s letter, the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps and Special Operations Command all confirmed they have disabled mobile advertising IDs on government-issued devices. However, that has only been recent for some service branches; the Air Force admitted in its letter to the members of Congress that it only directed disabling ad trackers in July.

Mobile advertising IDs, also known as MAIDs , are unique identifying numbers that go with specific devices. They are a key part of the data collected by mobile apps and can track location, common routes and habits, something that can be exploited by adversarial groups. Disabling those MAIDs is “a very simple and straightforward way that you can close a loophole,” according to Eva Galperin, Director of Cybersecurity for the Electronic Frontier Foundation. MAIDs aren’t the only way devices can be tracked, but are a major one.

“Minimizing the attack surface is always good, even if you don’t get the entire attack surface,” Galperin told Task & Purpose.

Another “particularly alarming” factor is that people are still using personal devices inside military installations and operating areas, exposing these places despite military restrictions. Wyden and Harrigon called on the office of the inspector general to see if personal devices are the main source of location data getting out and if so, the office “should recommend concrete policy changes to eliminate this vulnerability, enforce technical controls on personal devices in sensitive areas, and safeguard DoD personnel and OPSEC from commercial surveillance.”

Galperin noted that Wyden, who is on the Senate Intelligence Committee, releases letters like this to call attention to an urgent but classified matter.

Commercial data and location tracking features in apps have been an issue for the armed forces for years. U.S. Central Command issued stricter cybersecurity orders in December as part of the buildup of forces in the Middle East prior to the war with Iran. Since the war started, CENTCOM has updated those rules and warned troops that Iran was using “reactions, photos, and footage from the cellphones” of personnel to see how successful attacks are. Despite that, troops have continued using apps and Internet features with location data, including fitness apps.

Most recently, the Department of the Navy warned sailors and Marines that a “coordinated, multi-domain campaign” was underway to target them, including tracking people via their digital footprint. The notice advised, among other things, hiding one’s ties to the military online.

Existing commercial data from months prior to tracking being cut off could potentially still be useful to adversaries, but they don’t have real-time information, Galperin noted. But the continued use of personal phones and devices is the bigger risk, she said and military personnel overseas “probably shouldn’t be using them.”

title: Current ways of developing AI agents contribute to degradation of oversight
description: AI agents pose significant risks as they are granted increasing autonomy. A commonly proposed solution is human oversight and keeping a ''human in the loop'', but this is not a simple solution: Not only do current approaches to AI agent design impede effective human oversight, but the cognitive capacities required for it are also themselves degraded by extended use of AI systems. This position paper argues that current approaches to the development and deployment of AI agent systems do not support effective human oversight -- they contribute to its degradation. To address this, a top priority in the advancement of AI agents should be supporting the situated goals and cognitive requirements of effective human oversight, treating the human needs of overseers at the same level of importance as AI agent capability. To put this idea into practice, we connect work on automation and human-computer interaction to AI agent processes, outlining design-level affordances and organizational protocols that (1) support overseers in exercising critical judgement and (2) counteract the skill atrophy that arises from extended use of automation.

title: How Fast You Age During 40s May Predict Memory Lapses in Your 50s
description: As if middle-aged people don’t have enough to worry about
fullText:
As if middle-aged people don’t have enough to worry about

Midlife is a busy time—and it comes with plenty of stress. You likely have mounting responsibilities at work, kids that need your attention, parents that may need more care, increasing financial obligations, etc. When you add an aging mind and body on top of all that, it’s a lot to take on. Now, a new study suggests that how quickly you age during midlife can predict memory lapses a decade later.

To probe the relationship between biological aging and memory, researchers from Penn State University collected blood samples from 232 adults who were in their 40s during the 2000s. They tested the samples using two molecular clocks to determine biological age, as well as a third clock to measure the rate they were aging. This clock, called DunedinPACE, was developed by following a cohort of 1,000 people beginning in the 1970s and tracking changes in 19 biomarkers related to organ integrity every year since.

“Many of these tests are like your car’s odometer—they tell you how far you’ve gone in terms of age and how much aging-related change has accumulated,” study author David Almeida explained in a statement. “In this study, the useful measure turned out to be more like a car’s speedometer—a measure of how fast your body is aging during midlife.”

Around 10 years later, the researchers followed up with the group in a series of eight phone interviews, to find out how their memories were holding up. The participants were asked how often they experienced two different kinds of memory lapses: retrospective lapses (forgetting something in the past, like where they put their keys) and prospective lapses (forgetting to do something they planned to do, like take medication), as well as how often these glitches interfered with their lives.

“Though they may seem similar, prospective memory lapses are both less common and can be more serious than retrospective lapses,” Almeida said. “Misplacing your car keys can be irritating, but it’s often less harmful than missing doses of needed medication or accidentally skipping doctor’s appointments.”

When they looked for correlations between memory lapses and biological age, however, they didn’t find any. Instead they discovered that those who aged at a more rapid pace during middle age were 18 percent more likely to experience a prospective memory lapse. That means rapid agers may forget something on five more days each month, compared to their peers. And it could be a warning of things to come. According to past research, frequent prospective memory lapses may be associated with dementia later on.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you’re automatically doomed if you flake on a doctor’s appointment. Instead, the researchers say, it’s important to be mindful of any cognitive changes during this busy period. They also stress that you shouldn’t be shy about bringing up at your next doctor’s appointment.

“There are a lot of different physical causes of cognitive decline— from circulation issues to lack of sleep—but there are also a lot of effective solutions,” Almeida said. “If we catch problems early, we can enhance the quality of our lives, possibly for decades.”

title: Tyndall Effect
fullText:
The Tyndall effect is light scattering by particles in a colloid such as a very fine suspension (a sol). Also known as Tyndall scattering, it is similar to Rayleigh scattering, in that the intensity of the scattered light is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength, so blue light is scattered much more strongly than red light. An example in everyday life is the blue colour sometimes seen in the smoke emitted by motorcycles, in particular two-stroke machines where the burnt engine oil provides these particles.[1] The same effect can also be observed with tobacco smoke whose fine particles also preferentially scatter blue light.

Under the Tyndall effect, the longer wavelengths are transmitted more, while the shorter wavelengths are more diffusely reflected via scattering.[1] The Tyndall effect is seen when light-scattering particulate matter is dispersed in an otherwise light-transmitting medium, where the diameter of an individual particle is in the range of roughly 40 to 900 nm, i.e. somewhat below or near the wavelengths of visible light (400–750 nm).

It is particularly applicable to colloidal mixtures; for example, the Tyndall effect is used in nephelometers to determine the size and density of particles in aerosols[1] and other colloidal matter. Investigation of the phenomenon led directly to the invention of the ultramicroscope and turbidimetry.

It is named after the 19th-century physicist John Tyndall, who first studied the phenomenon extensively.[1]

Prior to his discovery of the phenomenon, Tyndall was primarily known for his work on the absorption and emission of radiant heat on a molecular level. In his investigations in that area, it had become necessary to use air from which all traces of floating dust and other particulates had been removed, and the best way to detect these particulates was to bathe the air in intense light.[2] In the 1860s, Tyndall did a number of experiments with light, shining beams through various gases and liquids and recording the results. In doing so, Tyndall discovered that when gradually filling the tube with smoke and then shining a beam of light through it, the beam appeared to be blue from the sides of the tube but red from the far end.[3] This observation enabled Tyndall to first propose the phenomenon which would later bear his name.

In 1902, the ultramicroscope was developed by Richard Adolf Zsigmondy (1865–1929) and Henry Siedentopf (1872–1940), working for Carl Zeiss AG. Curiosity about the Tyndall effect led them to apply bright sunlight for illumination and they were able to determine the size of 4 nm small gold nanoparticles that generate the cranberry glass colour. This work led directly to Zsigmondy's Nobel Prize for chemistry.[4][5]

The color of blue eyes is due to the Tyndall scattering of light by a translucent layer of turbid media in the iris containing numerous small particles of about 0.6 micrometers in diameter. These particles are finely suspended within the fibrovascular structure of the stroma or front layer of the iris.[6] Some brown irises have the same layer, except with more melanin in it. Moderate amounts of melanin make hazel, dark blue and green eyes.

In eyes that contain both particles and melanin, melanin acts as an important absorbing medium, effectively absorbing incident light within the layer and thereby significantly reducing both light reflection and scattering. In the absence of melanin, the layer is translucent, the incident light is no longer sufficiently absorbed but instead primarily interacts with the microscopic particles within the medium, resulting in random, isotropically distributed diffuse scattering. Under these conditions, a noticeable portion of the light that enters this translucent layer re-emerges via a radial scattered path. That is, there is backscatter, the redirection of the light waves back out to the open air.

Scattering takes place to a greater extent at shorter wavelengths. The longer wavelengths tend to pass straight through the translucent layer with unaltered paths of yellow light, and then encounter the next layer further back in the iris, which is a light absorber called the epithelium or uvea that is colored brownish-black. The brightness or intensity of scattered blue light that is scattered by the particles is due to this layer along with the turbid medium of particles within the stroma.

Thus, the longer wavelengths are not reflected (by scattering) back to the open air as much as the shorter wavelengths. Because the shorter wavelengths are the blue wavelengths, this gives rise to a blue hue in the light that comes out of the eye.[7][8] The blue iris is an example of a structural color because it relies only on the interference of light through the turbid medium to generate the color.

Blue eyes and brown eyes, therefore, are anatomically different from each other in a genetically non-variable[clarification needed] way because of the difference between turbid media and melanin.[citation needed] Both kinds of eye color can remain functionally separate despite being "mixed" together.[clarification needed]

When the day's sky is overcast, sunlight passes through the turbidity layer of the clouds, resulting in scattered, diffuse light on the ground (sunbeam). This exhibits Mie scattering instead of Tyndall scattering because the cloud droplets are larger than the wavelength of the light and scatters all colors approximately equally.[citation needed] Similarly, the term Tyndall effect is incorrectly applied to light scattering by large, macroscopic dust particles in the air as due to their large size, they do not exhibit Tyndall scattering.[1]

When the daytime sky is cloudless, the sky's color is blue due to Rayleigh scattering instead of Tyndall scattering. The primary scattering agents in the atmosphere are air molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen, and the characteristic dimensions of these molecules are much smaller than the wavelengths of visible light, thereby satisfying the conditions under which Rayleigh scattering is applicable.[9]

Another manifestation of Tyndall scattering can be seen in the blue colours exhibited by glacial meltwater on account of the suspended particles preferentially back scattering shorter wavelengths of the visible spectrum while absorbing longer wavelengths. Milky white rock flour combined with the blue tint caused by the Tyndall effect produces the characteristic “turquoise blue” often seen in meltwater streams. The actual shade of blue will ultimately be determined by the relative abundance of particulates capable of producing Tyndall scattering across the entire range of particle sizes suspended in the meltwater (see table below).

Rayleigh scattering is defined by a mathematical formula that requires the light-scattering particles to be far smaller than the wavelength of the light.[10] For a dispersion of particles to qualify for the Rayleigh formula, the particle sizes need to be below roughly 40 nanometres (for visible light),[citation needed] and the particles may be individual molecules.[10] Colloidal particles are bigger and are in the rough vicinity of the size of a wavelength of light. Tyndall scattering, i.e. colloidal particle scattering,[11] is much more intense than Rayleigh scattering due to the bigger particle sizes involved.[citation needed] The importance of the particle size factor for intensity can be seen in the large exponent it has in the mathematical statement of the intensity of Rayleigh scattering. If the colloid particles are spheroid, Tyndall scattering can be mathematically analyzed in terms of Mie theory, which admits particle sizes in the rough vicinity of the wavelength of light.[10] Light scattering by particles of complex shape are described by the T-matrix method.[12]
